Born in Russia on 12 July 1900. In March 1943 the family, Valentin, Zinaida, their four children and,
it seems, Zinaida's mother, were taken from the Luga district south of Leningrad to Germany;
Zinaida later wrote that they were “forcibly deported by the Wehrmacht because of front-line fighting.”
They were among some 2.8 million Soviet civilians brought into the Reich as forced labour,
a traffic that in the Luga district reached its height in 1943, when whole villages were taken.
They ended up at Weener, a small Ems town in East Frisia whose largest user of forced labour was the Klatte aircraft-parts
works, and they lived in a railway wagon at the station.
In April 1945 the war reached Weener. German troops blew up the Friesenbrücke, the railway bridge over the Ems beside
the town, to hold the Canadians on the river, and the Canadian 3rd Infantry Division came over the Dutch border from
Winschoten. The town changed hands on 22 or 23 April (local sources differ) .
The 23rd was the hardest day: shellfire killed children in the town, German artillery firing from Leer,
still in German hands across the river, fell short onto a family's shelter, and thirteen German soldiers,
several of them sailors of sixteen and seventeen, were killed and buried together.
That day, according to his death certificate, Valentin was shot at the station by a German soldier;
why is not recorded. The district's list of foreigners who died there gives only “shot by soldiers.”
He was buried in the new cemetery at Weener, row 3, grave 42, probably in one of the soldiers' common graves.
Weener's death register lists him as Ukrainian, under the spelling Maksinow.
Born 15 August 1916 at Savice, near Luga, south of Leningrad, daughter of Alex and Evdochia Kuleshowa.
Schooled at Luga, she taught at a village school until March 1943, when the Wehrmacht deported her and her four children,
Wasil, Aleksander, Robert and Nina, to Weener in East Frisia.
At Weener she worked as a cleaner, and the family lived in a railway wagon at the station.
Widowed on 23 April 1945, when Valentin was shot there in the last days of the fighting,
she stayed on, lived in displaced-persons camps at Westrhauderfehn, Varel and Bockhorn,
and married Wacław Stelmasik, a Polish former prisoner of war.
In July 1956 she flew to New York with her sons.
She died in New Jersey in 2008.
